findings.old_state: Hiring manager emails HR a PDF offer summary, and HR manually enters the employee into the HRIS system by hand 1-2 business days after the email.
findings.new_state: Hiring manager marks the offer as Accepted in the ATS, which automatically creates an employee record in the HRIS via API integration with no manual re-entry.

findings.old_state: HR prints and mails a paper welcome packet, tax forms (W-4, I-9), and benefits enrollment forms to the employee's home address, and the employee completes and returns them by mail or in person on day one.
findings.new_state: System-generated digital welcome packet, e-signature tax forms (W-4, I-9), and benefits enrollment are sent to the employee's personal email and completed digitally via e-signature before their start date.

findings.old_state: IT is notified via a separate email from HR after HRIS entry, and an IT technician manually provisions a laptop, email account, and system access following a printed checklist within 3-5 business days.
findings.new_state: An automated ticket is created in the IT provisioning system with role-based access templates, and laptops are shipped and accounts provisioned within 2 business days, tracked to completion in the dashboard.

findings.old_state: HR manually files paper forms in a physical cabinet and re-keys selected fields into the HRIS and payroll systems.
findings.new_state: Digital forms are stored directly in the document management system with no physical filing and no re-keying.

findings.old_state: Compliance training is assigned verbally by the manager with no automated tracking of completion, creating audit risk.
findings.new_state: Compliance training is auto-assigned in the Learning Management System (LMS) with due dates, automated reminders, and completion tracked and reportable for audit purposes.

findings.old_state: The hiring manager manually schedules first-week meetings and shadowing sessions by emailing relevant team members individually.
findings.new_state: First-week meetings and shadowing sessions are auto-scheduled based on a role-based onboarding template and synced to calendars, with options for the hiring manager to customize the template.

findings.old_state: Finance receives new-hire payroll setup information manually from HR, often by walking a paper form to the Finance office.
findings.new_state: A payroll setup record is created automatically from the HRIS entry with no manual form walked to Finance.

findings.old_state: There is no single system of record; HR, IT, and Finance each track onboarding status separately with no shared visibility.
findings.new_state: HR, IT, Finance, and the hiring manager all see the same real-time onboarding status dashboard serving as a single shared source of truth.

findings.old_state: The employee completes a paper Expense Claim Form (Form EX-12) by hand and staples the original receipts to the back of the form.
findings.new_state: The employee photographs each receipt in the SpendFlow app. Optical character recognition reads the amount, date and vendor and fills in the claim line.

findings.old_state: The employee's line manager reviews the claim and signs the form. Claims over $500 also need a second signature from the department head.
findings.new_state: Claims under $200 with no policy flags are approved automatically with no manager involvement. Claims from $200 to $2,000 go to the line manager. Claims over $2,000 need approval from both the line manager and the finance controller.

findings.old_state: Mileage is calculated manually at $0.45 per mile using the odometer readings written on the form.
findings.new_state: Mileage is calculated from the GPS trace recorded by the app at $0.50 per mile. Employees no longer enter odometer readings.

findings.old_state: Foreign currency expenses are converted at the exchange rate on the day the AP clerk keys the claim into the ledger, not the day the money was spent.
findings.new_state: Foreign currency expenses are converted at the daily rate from the central bank feed on the date of the transaction.

findings.old_state: Reimbursement is paid through the monthly payroll run on the 5th of the following month, so employees usually wait 30 to 40 days to be repaid.
findings.new_state: Approved claims are paid by direct deposit within 3 business days of final approval, instead of waiting for the monthly payroll run.

findings.old_state: If a receipt is lost, the employee must sign a written affidavit and the department head must countersign it before AP will process the line.
findings.new_state: An employee can attest to a lost receipt inside the app. The line is marked for audit, and each employee is limited to 3 attested lost receipts per quarter. Beyond that limit the claim is routed to the finance controller.

findings.old_state: There is no automated check for duplicate claims. Duplicates are caught only when a clerk happens to remember a previous submission.
findings.new_state: A duplicate detector screens every claim against the previous 12 months by amount, date and vendor before it reaches an approver.

findings.old_state: Finance reviews a random 5% sample of claims once per quarter.
findings.new_state: Finance samples 2% of auto-approved claims each month for manual review, replacing the old quarterly 5% sample.

findings.old_state: New suppliers are added through a chain of emails between the requesting team, Procurement and Finance, with no single system recording the state of a request.
findings.new_state: Vendors are onboarded through a self-service Vendor Portal that replaces the email chain and Vendor Master workbook, and requesters can see the status of every request in the portal.

findings.old_state: The procurement officer checks the vendor against the sanctions list by searching the OFAC website by hand and saves a screenshot of the result.
findings.new_state: Sanctions screening runs automatically through ComplyCheck at the moment of submission, and every active vendor is screened again each night.

findings.old_state: Bank details are verified by phoning the bank using the number printed on the bank letter.
findings.new_state: The bank account is verified with a micro-deposit test where the portal sends two small deposits and the vendor confirms the amounts.

findings.old_state: There is no risk assessment for vendors with annual spend under $25,000. Larger vendors receive a review that depends on which procurement officer picks up the request, so the depth of review varies.
findings.new_state: The portal assigns a risk tier based on expected annual spend and the type of data the vendor will handle, spanning Tier 1 (> $250k), Tier 2 ($25k to $250k), and Tier 3 (< $25k).

findings.old_state: Signed contracts are printed and kept in a physical binder in the Procurement office, and no one is warned when a contract is close to expiry.
findings.new_state: Signed contracts are stored in the contract repository, which sends renewal alerts to the contract owner 90 days before expiry.

findings.old_state: Vendors are never re-validated after onboarding, and sanctions status and bank details can go years without a check.
findings.new_state: Every vendor is re-validated each 12 months, and the portal sends automated reminders to vendors whose documents are about to expire.

findings.old_state: An internal audit found about 140 duplicate vendor records, mostly the same company entered twice under slightly different names.
findings.new_state: The portal checks the tax ID and the bank account number against existing records at submission, blocking matches and pointing the requester to the existing vendor.

citations.excerpt: New suppliers are added through a chain of emails between the requesting team, Procurement and Finance. The vendor list lives in a shared Excel workbook called Vendor Master, and there is no single system that records the state of a request.

Vendors are onboarded through a self-service Vendor Portal. The portal replaces the email chain and the Vendor Master workbook, and it creates the supplier record in the ERP system directly through an API.
Requesters can see the status of every request in the portal.
The procurement officer checks the vendor against the sanctions list by searching the OFAC website by hand and saves a screenshot of the result.
Sanctions screening runs automatically through ComplyCheck at the moment of submission, and every active vendor is screened again each night.
Bank details are verified by phoning the bank using the number printed on the bank letter.
The bank account is verified with a micro-deposit test. The portal sends two small deposits and the vendor confirms the amounts, which normally takes 2 days.

There is no risk assessment for vendors with annual spend under $25,000. Larger vendors receive a review that depends on which procurement officer picks up the request, so the depth of review varies from one vendor to another.
The portal assigns a risk tier based on expected annual spend and the type of data the vendor will handle.
Signed contracts are printed and kept in a physical binder in the Procurement office.
No one is warned when a contract is close to expiry, so some contracts lapse while the vendor continues to be paid.
Signed contracts are stored in the contract repository, which sends renewal alerts to the contract owner 90 days before expiry.
Vendors are never re-validated after onboarding. Sanctions status and bank details can go years without a check.
Every vendor is re-validated each 12 months, and the portal sends automated reminders to vendors whose documents are about to expire.
An internal audit found about 140 duplicate vendor records, mostly the same company entered twice under slightly different names.

The portal checks the tax ID and the bank account number against existing records at submission. A match blocks the request and points the requester to the existing vendor, which addresses the duplicate records found in the last audit.

findings.old_state: Anyone who noticed an outage called the service desk. Monitoring tools raised alarms on a wall display, but did not create tickets.
findings.new_state: A monitoring alert creates an incident in PagerRelay with a proposed severity and there is no need to phone the service desk.

findings.old_state: The service desk agent logged a ticket by hand and classified it as major or minor based on personal judgement, because there are no written severity definitions.
findings.new_state: Severity levels include SEV1, SEV2, and SEV3, each with a written definition so that two people classify the same issue the same way.

findings.old_state: For a major incident, the agent followed a printed phone tree and called the on-call engineer's mobile phone. If there was no answer after 10 minutes, the agent called the next engineer on the list.
findings.new_state: The on-call engineer is paged through the mobile app, then by SMS, then by phone call, and must acknowledge within 5 minutes or it escalates automatically to the secondary on-call and engineering manager.

findings.old_state: There was no incident commander, and engineers on the call decided among themselves who led the technical work.
findings.new_state: PagerRelay assigns an incident commander from a rotating roster who coordinates the work and does not make the technical changes.

findings.old_state: Updates went out by email to the all-it distribution list about every hour when someone remembered, and there was no public status page for customers.
findings.new_state: During a SEV1, the communications lead updates the public status page every 30 minutes until the incident is resolved.

findings.old_state: A written postmortem was required only when an outage lasted longer than 8 hours, was written in a Word document, stayed within engineering, and most incidents under 8 hours were never reviewed.
findings.new_state: A blameless postmortem is required within 5 business days for every SEV1 and SEV2 using a standard template stored in the engineering wiki, reviewed at the weekly reliability meeting, and action items are tracked in Jira.

findings.old_state: Engineers on the on-call list received no allowance and no formal rota, leading the same few senior engineers to answer most calls and suffer burnout.
findings.new_state: On-call duty rotates weekly across the whole engineering team, engineers receive an on-call stipend of $350 per week, and the rota is published a month ahead.

findings.old_state: Refund requests are handled one at a time by support agents through email, with no self-service option.
findings.new_state: Customers request refunds in the self-service Help Center.

findings.old_state: Finance pays refunds in a weekly batch every Thursday, with an average wait time of 9 days from request to money back.
findings.new_state: Approved refunds are paid in a daily run and reach the customer within 2 business days (under 2 days on average).

findings.old_state: Refunds are accepted within 14 days of delivery.
findings.new_state: The refund window has been extended to 30 days after delivery.

findings.old_state: Finance pays the refund to the original payment method only, and store credit is not offered.
findings.new_state: Customers can choose store credit instead of a payment to the original method, which carries a 10% bonus.

findings.old_state: A refund above $20 needs approval from a team lead via chat message, and a refund above $100 needs the support manager.
findings.new_state: A refund under $50 is approved instantly under certain conditions, a refund from $50 to $300 goes to a support agent, and a refund above $300 needs review by both the support manager and a fraud analyst.

findings.old_state: Fraud checks are limited to manual spot checks on 1 in 20 refunds, and agents rely on memory to recognise repeat refund requesters without a shared list.
findings.new_state: A fraud scoring model rates every request (scores above 0.8 trigger manual review), and the system flags a customer automatically after 3 refunds within 60 days with flags visible to every agent.

findings.old_state: Refund reasons are written as free text, preventing the company from reporting which products cause the most refunds.
findings.new_state: Customers choose reason codes from a fixed list for every request, enabling a weekly product-quality report.

Finance pays the refund to the original payment method only. Store credit is not offered.
Customers can choose store credit instead of a payment to the original method.   Store credit carries a 10% bonus.
Fraud checks are limited to manual spot checks on 1 in 20 refunds. Agents rely on memory to recognise customers who request refunds repeatedly. There is no shared   list of repeat refund requesters.

A fraud scoring model rates every request. Requests with a score above 0.8 are sent   for manual review even when they fall under the automatic limit. The system flags a   customer automatically after 3 refunds within 60 days, and the flag is visible to   every agent.
Refund reasons are written as free text, so the company cannot report which   products cause the most refunds.
Customers open the Help Center, selects the order and chooses a reason code   from a fixed list.
Reason codes are captured for every request. A weekly product-quality report shows   which items generate the most refunds, so merchandising can act on the data.
